# Here is a solution using a Python 3.11 feature called bit swap. A
# bit swap is a low-level optimization that is hard to see and hard not to
# get right. Computers (like humans) have a natural tendency to move things
# to a higher position when given the chance. For example, add one to a number
# in the 5 bits is extremely easy (just put a '1' before the first bit and a
# '0' after the last bit), but adding the same value to the 9 bit version is a
# little trickier. Swapping the bits that are important, and those that are not,
# makes things a lot easier. Here, we don't actually swap the bits, but we do
# use the fact that when two numbers just differ in a few bits, the operations
# that affect those few bits can in one direction give you the result you want
# without actually swappping the bits. The only bit operations needed in the
# solution below are LEFT SHIFT and NOT.

    small_in_numerals = num & target
    small_in_numerals |= (maxcount - count) << (len(bin(small_in_numerals)) - count_in_k_numerals)

    # Add the count for k in the numerals of the target number
    tree = 0
    j = 10
    for i in range(5):
      mask = 1 << i
      tree += mask * (1 if target & mask else 0)
      j = 10 - j
    target_end = min(target & small_in_numerals, tree)
    count += small_in_numerals == target_end
